meta.description: C.S. Lewis never wrote it. The saying is an anonymous modern aphorism first attested in 2004; the Lewis credit appears only in 2011, decades after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Comparison is the thief of joy'?
meta.ogDescription: Not C.S. Lewis, Roosevelt, or Twain. It's an anonymous modern saying first attested around 2004 — the Lewis credit surfaces only in 2011.

answer.label: Not C.S. Lewis — a modern anonymous saying
answer.sourceLine: No work by C.S. Lewis contains this line. Quote Investigator finds the exact wording only in the mid-2000s as an anonymous saying — and the earliest source to use it, Curt Cloninger’s 2004 Connect2God, itself says only “Somebody once said…” The Lewis credit does not appear until 2011, and QI judges it — along with the Roosevelt and Twain credits — “currently unsupported.”

source.excerpt: Somebody once said that comparison is the thief of joy.
trail: Quote Investigator finds the exact wording first in Curt Cloninger’s 2004 Connect2God, where it is disclaimed as “Somebody once said,” and conjectures the saying was already circulating anonymously.
The credit to C.S. Lewis first appears in 2011, in Marian Jordan’s The Girlfriends’ Guidebook — nearly half a century after Lewis’s death in 1963, per QI.
The rival credits followed later still — Theodore Roosevelt in 2012 and Mark Twain in 2013 — a classic sign of a “magnet” quote drifting onto famous names, per QI.
QI concludes the ascriptions to Roosevelt, Twain, and Lewis are all “currently unsupported.”

author.name: C.S. Lewis
author.heading: About the credited author
author.bio: Clive Staples Lewis was an Oxford and Cambridge literary scholar and the author of The Chronicles of Narnia, Mere Christianity, and The Screwtape Letters. His warmth and quotability have made him one of the internet’s biggest magnets for feel-good aphorisms — many, like this one, that he never wrote. The line does not appear in any of his published works, letters, or talks.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly credited to
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet” quote: an anonymous modern saying that has been pinned, in turn, onto three famous names, none of whom can be shown to have said it.

items.why: The credit first appears in 2011, in Marian Jordan’s The Girlfriends’ Guidebook — nearly 50 years after Lewis died in 1963. The line is in none of his works, and Quote Investigator calls the ascription unsupported.
The most viral modern credit, but it surfaces only in 2012 — over 90 years after Roosevelt’s death — with no documented source in his speeches or writings, per QI.
A later credit still, appearing in 2013, with no basis in Twain’s works — a common landing spot for orphan aphorisms, per QI.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented use, in 2004, already treats the line as anonymous — “Somebody once said” — and Quote Investigator finds no support for any of the famous attributions.

context.heading: Why the confusion
lead: The sentiment — that measuring yourself against others drains your contentment — is old and widely felt, which is exactly why it attaches so easily to admired names. But a familiar idea is not evidence of a specific author. The exact epigram “comparison is the thief of joy” is only documented from the mid-2000s onward.

When a saying has no home, it tends to drift toward whoever lends it the most authority. Here that pull produced three different famous fathers in quick succession — Lewis (2011), Roosevelt (2012), and Twain (2013) — a pattern that itself signals fabrication rather than fact.
context.pull: An anonymous line in 2004; three famous fathers by 2013.
